title: Pushed or jiggled spheres do not reach densest packing

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Pushed or jiggled spheres do not reach densest packing

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Unlike identical coins in two dimensions, which readily form the densest hexagonal packing when pushed together, balls in three dimensions pushed together or jiggled almost always get stuck and essentially never reach the densest repetitive packing, which seems obtainable only by careful one-by-one placement.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But if one just tries pushing balls together they almost always get stuck, and never take on anything like the arrangement shown.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 7, “Mechanisms in Programs and Nature”; section “The Problem of Satisfying Constraints” (from p. 342), p. 349. Scope: packing of identical spheres and circles under physical compression or agitation

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch07-18: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.66

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Packing density and order are standard observables, and existing experiments and simulations cover many protocols. Public records are scattered and do not uniformly span the claim's protocol space. They can resolve typical behavior under defined conditions but not the absolute or almost-always wording.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For public experimental and simulated packing trajectories, compare final packing fraction and crystalline order after compression or agitation of monodisperse disks and spheres against the known densest values. Frequent spontaneous attainment in spheres would refute the claim; robust jamming below crystalline order across protocols would support it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Careful one-by-one placement is not a sharply bounded intervention.

Essentially never cannot be established from finite trials.

Results depend strongly on friction, container geometry, polydispersity, and agitation protocol.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The target densities are mathematical and the two-dimensional case is classical, so the comparison itself is sharp. Laboratory results on random close packing are public but dispersed, and they show both jamming under simple agitation and crystallization under more careful driving. The claim is therefore decidable for specified protocols and not as an unqualified never across every way of jiggling.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare measured packing fractions of identical disks under lateral compression, and of identical spheres under compression or vibration, with the proved maxima (hexagonal packing in two dimensions, about 0.74 in three). Disks reaching the hexagonal fraction, and spheres remaining well below the three-dimensional maximum under ordinary pushing and jiggling, would support the claim; spheres that routinely crystallize into the densest packing under those protocols would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Outcome depends on the agitation protocol: shearing and slow annealing can crystallize spheres that gentle jiggling leaves jammed.

Experimental packing fractions are scattered across papers rather than held in one open campaign.
